one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens the year by marking two milestones: the 30th anniversary of Edsa 1 (Feb 22-25, upcoming) and the 15th of Edsa 2 (Jan 16-20, just passed) -- the SC having characterized them as 'extra' and 'intra' constitutional ways of upholding democracy and the great libertarian and egalitarian principles. He begins with Edsa 2, whose constitutionality was upheld unanimously 13-0 in Estrada vs Desierto (March 2, 2001) -- with Davide and Panganiban inhibiting. As a participant in Edsa 2, Panganiban kept a diary; some passages were highlighted in his Feb 19, 2002 UST Central Seminary speech, later published as Chapter 11 of his book 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- printed by the SC, never sold in any bookstore, and contrary to critics' claims never 'withdrawn'; copies are in archives like the Court library. He recounts: the prosecutors' walkout on Jan 16, 2001 was triggered by the Senate's 11-10 vote refusing to open the so-called second envelope allegedly containing damning evidence of a P3.3 billion secret account under 'Jose Velarde.' Estrada vs Desierto records: 'In disgust, Senator Pimentel resigned as Senate President. The (11-10) ruling made at 10:00 pm was met by a spontaneous outburst of anger that hit the streets of the metropolis. By midnight, thousands had assembled at the Edsa Shrine and speeches full of sulphur were delivered against Estrada and the 11 senators.' On Jan 18, a 10-kilometer human chain of candle-bearers formed from the Ninoy Aquino monument on Ayala Avenue to the Edsa Shrine to symbolize solidarity demanding Estrada's resignation; students and teachers walked out of Metro Manila classrooms; speakers at the rallies, 'all masters of the physics of persuasion,' attracted more and more people. On Jan 19, AFP Chief of Staff Gen. Angelo Reyes defected and announced -- in the presence of all armed-services heads -- that the '130,000-strong members of the armed forces were withdrawing their support to the government.' A little later, PNP head Panfilo Lacson made a similar announcement; several Cabinet and sub-Cabinet officials followed. With AFP, PNP, and Cabinet allegiance shifted to Arroyo, Estrada could no longer govern -- but Arroyo could not yet legally lead either. There was no functioning government. On Jan 20, Panganiban woke at 4 am to a TV panel grimly announcing that Cardinal Sin via Msgr. Villegas was pleading with demonstrators not to march to Malacañang. The demonstrators refused -- they would storm the presidential enclave by 6 am and forcefully oust Estrada. Aghast at the violence and bloodshed that would ensue, with images of past Mendiola massacres haunting him, Panganiban called Davide at 5:30 am: the imminent encounter would be bloody and chaotic; Estrada could no longer govern; Arroyo could only take over by declaring a revolutionary government, which would obliterate the Constitution; the situation was ripe for a coup d'état. To avoid a power vacuum and a coup, he asked Davide to swear in Arroyo by 12 noon -- extraordinary crisis needed an extraordinary solution. When Davide (and later other justices and media) asked for legal justification to swear in the VP while the incumbent was still physically in office, Panganiban replied that while the constitutional text did not expressly cover the critical situation, the CJ could lean on the grand maxim Salus populi est suprema lex -- the welfare of the people is the supreme law -- precisely to save the Constitution and democratic system from destruction. To cut the long story short, Davide agreed and swore in Arroyo at 12:29 pm of that day. The forward-pointer: next Sunday will discuss how this milestone -- started by Panganiban's proposal to Davide and approved by the justices to swear in an 'acting president' -- metamorphosed into an oath for a 'President' (without 'acting'), and how the metamorphosis was unanimously judged constitutional 13-0 (Davide and Panganiban inhibiting).
